preamble: Nasalization of [i] to [ĩ] usually arises when the vowel absorbs an adjacent nasal consonant, though it can also arise without a nasal source. In Portuguese, Latin -īn- yielded a nasal vowel (fīnem > fim [ˈfĩ]); Old French nasalized /i/ before /n/ or /m/ (fin [fĩn], later lowered to [fɛ̃]). In Hindi and Punjabi a vowel before a lost nasal became a long nasal vowel (Sanskrit siñcati > Hindi sī̃cnā), and Hindi also shows nasalization without a nasal source (Prakrit iṭṭā > ī̃ṭ 'brick'). Southern Min colloquial readings show lexical nasalization of /i/ (鼻 Quanzhou phī [pʰi] vs Xiamen phīⁿ [pʰĩ]).

examples.note: Via Old Galician-Portuguese fim/fin; the coda nasal was absorbed into the vowel, which surfaces as [ĩ] in both Brazilian and European Portuguese.

examples.to: Old Galician-Portuguese vỹo, Ancarese Galician vĩo
examples.note: Intervocalic n was lost after nasalizing the preceding i; standard Portuguese later developed vinho with a palatal nasal.
Old French nasalized /i/, /u/, /y/ before /n/ or /m/; in Modern French [ĩ] was lowered to [ɛ̃] (fin /fɛ̃/), while feminine fine /fin/ kept an oral vowel once the nasal stood before a vowel.
Inherited via Prakrit siṃcaï and Apabhramsa siṃcei; the nasal of the cluster was lost and the preceding vowel became long and nasalized.
Nasalization without a nasal consonant in the source, together with compensatory lengthening on degemination of ṭṭ.
The anusvara nasal was absorbed into a long nasal vowel; ਸਿੰਘ siṅgh is a doublet that keeps the nasal consonant. The initial ś is irregular.

examples.from: Middle Chinese 鼻 bjijH 'nose' (Quanzhou colloquial phī /pʰi/)
examples.note: Colloquial nasalization of /i/ without a nasal consonant in the source; the literary reading is pi̍t.
